title: Lok Adalats
lead: India's ==oldest and most widely used institutionalised ADR mechanism== — rooted in panchayat-style dispute settlement, formalised by statute to relieve the judiciary's chronic backlog. ==‘Justice delayed is justice denied, but justice hurried without fairness is justice buried.’==

sections.title: Lok Adalat v Permanent Lok Adalat

blocks.text: Ordinary Lok Adalats have ==no independent adjudicatory jurisdiction== — they cannot impose a decision; their entire function is to facilitate a ==consent-based settlement==. ==Permanent Lok Adalats are the sole exception==, holding both conciliatory and binding decision-making powers over public utility disputes within prescribed pecuniary limits.

items.title: Matters Lok Adalats CAN Take Up
bullets: Any ==pending case or pre-litigation matter== where parties agree, or the court finds it suitable
==Civil disputes== — property, partition suits, land acquisition compensation
Matrimonial and family disputes (==maintenance and mutual-consent== matters commonly settled)
==Motor Accident Claims Tribunal (MACT)== cases — one of the largest single categories nationally
Bank recovery, ==cheque bounce (s.138 NI Act)==, labour disputes
==Compoundable criminal offences== under the BNS/CrPC framework
==Public utility service disputes== — exclusively before Permanent Lok Adalats

items.title: Matters EXCLUDED
bullets: ==Non-compoundable criminal offences== — murder, rape, serious offences against the State
Offences against ==women and children== where compromise is disallowed — dowry death, certain ==POCSO== matters
Disputes on ==title to property== in categories requiring adjudication rather than compromise

head: Case
Key holding
rows: Lok Adalats can pass an award ==only on the basis of a compromise== — ==no power to adjudicate on merits==.
An award is ==as good as a civil court decree==, executable and binding, and ==cannot ordinarily be challenged== except by writ on limited grounds.

head: Country / model
Practice
rows: Court-annexed mediation with ==trained professional mediators and strict timelines==
Judges can ==mandate ADR referral==; strong small-claims infrastructure for low-value disputes
Localised, ==community-embedded resolution centres== integrated with formal courts

items: ==Quantity over quality — ‘assembly-line justice’==: pressure to clear crores of cases per National Lok Adalat raises concerns of rushed settlements with inadequate scrutiny of consent or fairness.
==Coercion and unequal bargaining power==: weaker parties (claimants against insurers or banks) may accept lower amounts to avoid prolonged litigation — undermining voluntariness.
==Limited awareness== among rural and marginalised litigants of eligibility and of the ==finality== of an award.
==No appeal mechanism== — s.21's bar leaves only the narrow, expensive writ remedy, defeating the purpose of a quick, low-cost forum.
==Repeat/recurring case types dominate== — undefended or semi-mechanical categories (cheque bounce, MACT, bank recovery) raise the question of ==bulk clearance vs substantive resolution==.
==Resource and capacity constraints== — DLSAs and Taluk committees understaffed, dependent on retired judicial officers and volunteering advocates.
==Permanent Lok Adalats under-utilised== — low awareness of the pre-litigation compulsory conciliation route.
==Data and monitoring gaps== — little granular data on ==post-settlement compliance== (whether awarded amounts are actually paid).
==National Lok Adalats== on fixed dates across all court tiers since 2015, often ==themed by subject-matter== each month — improving predictability and outreach.
==e-Lok Adalats / Virtual Lok Adalats== — video-conferencing access benefiting elderly, disabled and remote litigants; adopted at scale during the pandemic and retained.

==Jharkhand's 99.95% disposal rate== in the first National Lok Adalat of 2025 — showing that strong SLSA coordination and ==pre-identification of settlement-ready cases== dramatically raise efficiency.
==Legal Aid Defence Counsel System (LADCS)== — NALSA's scheme professionalising the panel and improving representation quality.
==Mediation Act, 2023 synergy== — a layered ADR ecosystem with the ==Mediation Council of India== for standard-setting.
==Strengthen consent safeguards== — a cooling-off period or brief counsel review before finalising high-value or vulnerable-party settlements
==Expand Permanent Lok Adalats== — awareness campaigns and periodic rationalisation of pecuniary limits
==Institutionalise post-award monitoring== — a NALSA-led compliance tracker measuring ==real, not paper, resolution==
==Deepen digital access== — vernacular e-Lok Adalats, assisted kiosks at Gram Nyayalayas/Panchayats, e-Courts integration
==Capacity building== — funding and staffing for DLSAs/Taluk committees; more trained panel lawyers and PLVs
==Targeted outreach== to rural, tribal and economically weaker populations
==Data transparency== — publish ==case-category-wise== data, not just aggregate disposal figures
==Harmonise with the Mediation Act, 2023== — clear referral pathways, avoiding forum confusion
